newsitem.title: IRAN: Storm clouds gather over Khatami's cabinet list.
newsitem.headline: Storm clouds gather over Khatami's cabinet list.

text.p: Storm clouds are starting to gather over some of moderate Iranian President Mohammad Khatami's choices for cabinet positions.

Khatami's opponents in the conservative-led Majlis, or parliament, were reported in Iranian newspapers on Wednesday as saying they would be reluctant to pass a necessary vote of confidence on a core of potentially reformist ministers.

The 54-year-old Shi'ite cleric, with a reputation for political openness and elected into office on a mandate of introducing social and economic reforms, on Tuesday presented his list of 22 cabinet nominees to the 270-seat Majlis.
Deputies will start debating the merits of each of Khatami's cabinet nominees and their programme on Tuesday.

But some conservative parliament members are already indicating that Khatami could be in for a disappointment on a number of key portfolios including the sensitive positions of culture, interior and even foreign affairs ministers.

"I don't think that Mr. Khatami is going to be able to perform the miracles the people expect of him. I'm rather worried about the next four years," rightist deputy Ahmad Rasoolnejad told the Iran News daily paper.

Khatami's landslide election victory in May was mainly secured by the support of youth, women and middle-class Iranians on expectations the moderate cleric would ease daily restrictions in life, such as a strict Islamic dress code.
His nomination of Ataollah Mohajerani, a close aide of former president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, as minister of culture and Islamic guidance provoked strong opposition.

"Mohajerani does not deserve to be a member of the cabinet. One who has been the inventor of direct talks with America is detrimental to the foreign image of the government," the conservative Resalat evening paper reported.
"We will have to clear up his mess (if appointed)," the paper said in a stinging editorial.

The 43-year-old Mohajerani, trained as a historian, has faced increasingly sharp criticism from conservatives after he advocated direct talks with the United States in 1990 and pressed for more cultural freedoms.
"He (Mohajerani) is very unlikely to be approved of by the Majlis and he will most probably be replaced," an unnamed parliament member told the Tehran Times.
The culture ministry plays a key role in domestic life in Iran since it has power over what books and films can be produced and the extent of media freedom.
If Khatami fails to secure his appointee at culture, high expectations among the electorate of new freedoms in the 18-year-old Islamic republic could be dashed, analysts said.

"The weak point of the cabinet is that some members do not have a strong ideological basis and their backgrounds show tolerance to the world arrogance (the West)," the conservative Abrar newspaper said in an editorial.
Abrar quoted conservative parliament member Nafiseh Fayazbakhsh as saying that problems could arise over the posts of culture, interior, oil and education ministers.
Iran News also reported that conservatives in parliament had warned they would block the nomination of both Mohajerani and interior ministry nominee Abdollah Nouri.
Nouri, a cleric and former interior minister, heads a pro-Khatami faction in parliament.
Local conservative papers have said Khatami's candidate for foreign affairs -- United Nations ambassador Kamal Kharrazi -- could also be rejected by parliament members.

"It is not fitting that a person who has lived in the United States, whether as a student or as U.N. ambassador, should be in charge of the foreign policy of a nation that considers the United States its greatest enemy," the hardline Jomhuri Eslami said prior to Khatami's cabinet submission on Tuesday.
The 53-year-old Kharrazi lived in the United States from 1972 to 1979, earning a doctorate in education, before being appointed U.N. envoy in New York in 1989.
Moderate, pro-Khatami parliament members said they expected the Majlis to accept the president's nominations because the list included people from across the political spectrum.
